title: On one Spanish island, people whistle whole sentences to each other
hook: An island where people once whistled messages 5 km across the valleys

open.title: The island where whistles once carried words 5 km away
open.line: On Spain's La Gomera, people use tongue, lips and hands to whistle across the valleys.

summary: Silbo Gomero, from Spain's La Gomera, is Spanish turned into whistles. UNESCO listed it as heritage in 2009.

text: On Spain's La Gomera, people use tongue, lips and hands to whistle across the valleys.
It's not a tune. It's a sentence.
Deep ravines cut through the whole island.
These whistles reportedly carried news up to 5 km.

panels.text: What can you even say with a whistle? Tweet tweet?

text: Actually, it isn't a made-up code.
It's the islanders' Spanish, turned straight into whistles.
Five vowels become two whistles, and consonants become four.
Pitch and breaks tell them apart. With practice, you can say anything.
UNESCO calls it the only fully developed whistled language used by a community of over 22,000.
It joined the heritage list in 2009.
But many born from 1950 to 1980 understood it but couldn't whistle it.
So since 1999, it's been taught in schools.
In a 2005 Nature study, whistlers' brains processed it in language areas.
To everyone else, it was just whistling.

sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Silbo Gomero
Carreiras et al. (2005), Linguistic perception: neural processing of a whistled language, Nature 433
